name: Sam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Brightwire, an electrical wholesaler: cable, sockets, LED panels, fuse boards, all the stuff electricians pick up at seven in the morning on their way to a job. My mornings are forecasting, so I look at what sold last week, what big building jobs are coming and what copper prices are doing. Then I place orders with about twenty manufacturers and spend the afternoon on the phone sorting out late deliveries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of it, guessing that every electrician in town will want the same smart thermostat in March. Last year I built my own reorder tool with an AI assistant, which looks at sales and suggests orders, and it cut my Monday work from four hours to one. What drains me is copper prices jumping around and the late shipments from overseas, which nobody can fix, not even a clever computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd tell people at work the tools are still handy and they should use them for the boring stuff. Online I'd post something like, so much for the robot uprising, enjoy your spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, even good. I'm already the person in the office who uses AI most, so I'd keep a small edge without the job disappearing. The part of me that likes new toys would be a bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep improving my reorder tool, maybe hook it up to the copper price feed so it warns me before prices jump. I'd offer to show Gary and the other two buyers how it works, because they'd save hours too. Money-wise we'd carry on, keep the four months of savings, keep paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, like a film that didn't live up to the trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Gary. How do you think he'd take it if you showed him the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd roll his eyes and then quietly use it when I'm not looking. I like Gary. My colleague Gary has bought cable for twenty-five years from memory and a notebook, and he knows things about suppliers no computer ever will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your plans change if AI really stalled here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe I'd stop reading three AI newsletters a week and spend that time with my son Lucas on his football. Honestly, that might be the best part of this picture.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed and tell colleagues the tools are still handy for boring jobs. Online I'd joke that the robot uprising never came.
S0.think: It's fine, even good, because I keep a small edge as the office's biggest AI user without the job disappearing. The part of me that likes new toys would be a bit bored.
S0.do: Keeps improving his own AI reorder tool and links it to copper price data. Teaches the other three buyers, including Gary, to use it, and keeps the four months of savings and mortgage as they are.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly let down, like a film that didn't live up to its trailer.
S0.quote: My colleague Gary has bought cable for twenty-five years from memory and a notebook, and he knows things about suppliers no computer ever will.
S0.fieldNote: Sam is the early adopter in his office and already built his own forecasting tool. He is mildly disappointed by a calm future, which shows how much he enjoys change. His respect for his old-school colleague Gary is genuine, not polite.

steps.text: Link the home-built reorder tool to live copper prices
Show Gary and the other buyers how the reorder tool works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why workers need a say in how AI comes in. At work I'd push for the time saved to go to people, like a four-day week, not just fewer staff. Online I'd post about it, I'm one of those people who posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do fine. I'm already doing half my job with AI, so I'd be one of the people running the new systems, not the one replaced by them. What worries me is Gary and the two others, who'd find it much harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my manager, Paula, and offer to lead the AI rollout for the buying team, with a proper title and a bit more pay. I'd join the union branch, which I've been meaning to do, and push for a deal on retraining and hours. And I'd keep learning, maybe a short online course on supply chain data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. A bit guilty that it's good for me and bad for people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. What would you actually do for Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure he's in the room when the system is set up, because his supplier knowledge is gold. If they try to push him out, I'd argue in the union that Gary trains the AI system instead of being replaced by the AI system. Whether they'd listen, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your spending at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. If I got the lead role, we'd put the extra money into savings rather than a new car. Ana, my partner, is a primary teacher, so we're not rich, but we're steady.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a say in how AI comes in, and push for the time saved to become a four-day week rather than fewer staff. I'd post about it online too.
S1.think: I'd do fine, since I already do half my job with AI and would run the new systems. My worry is Gary and the other two buyers, who'd find it much harder.
S1.do: Offers his manager, Paula, to lead the AI rollout for buying, with a title and a raise. Joins the union branch to push for retraining and shorter hours, and takes a short online course in supply chain data.
S1.feel: Calm and mostly excited, with guilt that the change is good for him and bad for colleagues he likes.
S1.quote: I'd argue in the union that Gary trains the AI system instead of being replaced by the AI system.
S1.fieldNote: Sam is a rare mix: eager adopter and committed union voice. His politics show up as a demand to share time saved, not just to protect jobs. He knows he benefits from this picture and the guilt is real.

steps.text: Offer to lead the buying team's AI rollout for a raise
Join the union branch and push for a four-day week
Take a short online course in supply chain data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the gains have to be shared, through taxes on the AI companies and proper income support. This is the moment unions and governments exist for. I'd be at protests, and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being the AI guy doesn't save me here. If the AI can do any thinking work, Brightwire needs maybe one person to watch it, and they might not need that. My edge disappears in two years, and that's frightening, even for someone who likes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031, so the hands-on trades last three years longer than desk jobs. I'd sign up for an evening electrical course straight away, because I know the products inside out and half my customers are electricians who'd take me on. We'd put every spare bit into savings, aiming to go from four months to eight, and drop the holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head is racing, but it's a racing-to-do-something feeling, not a frozen one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be training as an electrician in your mid-forties. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harder than I'd like, my knees aren't twenty. But I know Dev, who runs a small electrical firm and buys from us every week, and he's always saying he can't find people. I'd ask Dev for Saturday work while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031, when the robots come too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in the same boat as everyone, and that's where the politics matters. I'm not going to outrun AGI alone, I can only buy a few years as an electrician. A few years is still worth having when you've got two kids at school.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that the gains must be shared, through taxes on AI companies and proper income support. I'd go to protests and say so online.
S2.think: Being the AI guy doesn't save me: Brightwire might need one person to watch the system, or none. My edge disappears in two years, which frightens me even though I like change.
S2.do: Signs up for an evening electrical course straight away and asks a customer, Dev, for Saturday work while training. Puts every spare amount into savings to grow from four to eight months, drops the family holiday, and joins protests for shared gains.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a racing mind that pushes him to act rather than freeze.
S2.quote: I'm not going to outrun AGI alone, I can only buy a few years as an electrician.
S2.fieldNote: Sam sees immediately that his AI skill stops mattering once AI can do the whole job. He uses the three-year robot lag deliberately, moving into the trade he already knows from the customer side. He is clear-eyed that personal moves only buy time and that the rest is political.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical course and ask Dev for Saturday work
Drop the holiday and grow savings from four to eight months
Join protests calling for AI taxes and income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and a warning is useless unless you act. I'd push at work and in the union for a plan for every buyer and warehouse worker. Online I'd keep banging on about sharing the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay for the first few years, probably better than okay. Companies will want someone to set up the AI buying systems before 2031, and that could be me. After that, the buying job's gone, so I'd use the good years to set up what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on the AI project at Brightwire and get paid properly for it, maybe even freelance it to other wholesalers on weekends. With the extra money, I'd start a part-time electrical course in year two or three and pay for it myself. I'd aim to be a qualified electrician by 2031, three years ahead of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More interesting than scary, but I know where the road ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be setting up the systems that replace buyers. How do you square that with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. If I don't set up the AI buying system, a consultant from outside will, and the consultant won't care about Gary. At least I'd push for proper notice and retraining for everyone, and I'd tell people honestly what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about the weekend freelancing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would say fine, for a year, then she'd want her husband back. She's right. I'd set a limit, maybe fifteen weekends, and the money goes into the course and savings, not toys.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning that's useless unless you act, and push at work and in the union for a plan for every buyer and warehouse worker. I'd keep posting about sharing the gains.
S3.think: The first few years would be good for me, setting up AI buying systems before 2031. After that the buying job is gone, so I'd use the good years to build what comes next.
S3.do: Takes on Brightwire's AI project for proper pay and freelances it to other wholesalers on up to fifteen weekends. Pays for a part-time electrical course from year two or three, aiming to qualify by 2031.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more curious than scared, knowing where the road ends.
S3.quote: If I don't set up the AI buying system, a consultant from outside will, and the consultant won't care about Gary.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Sam room to profit from the change before it hits, which sits awkwardly with his politics, and he says so. His justification is that he'd do it more humanely than an outsider. He plans to qualify as an electrician by the AGI date, using the robot lag on purpose.

steps.text: Lead Brightwire's AI buying project for proper pay
Freelance AI setup to other wholesalers for fifteen weekends
Pay for a part-time electrical course and qualify by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right if we start now: tax the gains, cut working hours, fund training. I'd say it at work, in the union and online. Honestly, I'd be one of the hopeful voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a career and a half. I'd be 53 when AGI arrives and the kids would be grown. I think I'd have a good run with the AI work and then move into something hands-on without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the AI rollout at Brightwire over the next few years and save hard, maybe putting the extra into an index fund for the kids. Around 2030 I'd start electrical training at a normal pace, evenings, no rush. I'd keep pushing the union for a shorter week, because if the work shrinks, the hours should shrink with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even quite hopeful, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound quite relaxed. Is there anything in this picture that does get to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What gets to me is whether the government actually uses the ten years. I can handle my own family, but if half the town loses their desk jobs in 2036 and nothing's ready, that's a mess for everyone. My kids would be starting out right then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Lucas to learn to use AI like a pencil, but also to learn to fix, build or care for something real. Lucas likes taking bikes apart, so maybe that's his thing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we start now by taxing the gains, cutting hours and funding training. I'd be one of the hopeful voices at work, in the union and online.
S4.think: Ten years is a career and a half; I'd be 53 when AGI arrives, with the kids grown. I'd have a good run with AI work and then move into something hands-on without panic.
S4.do: Leads the AI rollout at Brightwire and saves the extra pay, putting some into an index fund for the children. Starts electrical training at an easy pace around 2030, and keeps pushing the union for a shorter week.
S4.feel: Calm and even hopeful, with a nagging doubt about whether government uses the time.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Lucas to learn to use AI like a pencil, but also to learn to fix, build or care for something real.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Sam is the most relaxed he gets, seeing a full arc from AI work to a trade. His worry shifts from himself to the town and his children's generation. He reads the AI-first, robots-later order as a simple plan: profit from AI now, move into hands-on work later.

steps.text: Put the extra pay from AI work into an index fund
Start evening electrical training around 2030 at an easy pace
Keep pushing the union for a shorter working week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone who loves this stuff can't move fast enough in two years. What would help is income support while you retrain, and fast-track trade courses that don't take four years. If I could qualify as an electrician in eighteen months with part of my wage covered, I'd be fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel responsible. I do, a bit. Every hour I save with AI is an hour my company might decide it doesn't need to pay someone for.

headlineQuote: Every hour I save with AI is an hour my company might decide it doesn't need to pay someone for.
portrait: Sam Diaz, 43, buys cable, lighting and fittings for Brightwire, an electrical wholesaler, and is the office's keenest AI user, having built his own reorder tool. He is calm in the first two pictures and expects to lead the change, though he feels guilty about colleagues like Gary. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious, and he would use the three-year robot gap to retrain as an electrician through a customer's firm. With five or ten years he would profit from AI work first, then move into the trade, growing calmer as the time grows. His progressive politics run through every picture: share the gains, shorten the week, fund retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even someone who loves the technology can't change careers in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Income support during retraining and fast-track trade courses, so he could qualify as an electrician in about eighteen months with part of his wage covered.
